ad_past_pln:
“China has issued the National Strategy on Climate Change Adaptation. The strategy laid out clear guiding thoughts and principles for climate change adaptation from 214 to 22, as a guidance for various policies and institutional arrangements; set out specific adaptation goals such as significant enhancement of adaptation capacity, full implementation of key tasks, and basic formation of regional framework for adaptation; identified key tasks in seven areas, including infrastructure, agriculture, water resources, coastal regions and coastal waters, forests and other ecosystems, human health, tourism and other industries; proposed adaptation tasks with respective emphasis for urbanized areas, agricultural development areas, and ecological security areas. Pursuant to this strategy, departments concerned and local provinces and cities have carried out a considerable amount of comprehensive and systematic work, adjusted and improved relevant policies and institutional arrangements, and proactively implemented policies and actions on climate change adaptation, which yields positive results.” (p. 22) 

Consolidate the foundation of adaptation research and technological development: “In response to industry and local needs, basic research has been carried out, including the assessment of climate change impacts and disaster risks and the mechanism of adapting climate change. The China National Assessment Report on Management and Adaptation to Risks of Extreme Weather and Climate Events and Disasters was completed. The Research on National Science and Technology Development Strategy for Adapting to Climate Change was published, which clarified the basic framework of scientific and technological system with Chinese characteristics for adapting to climate change, and suggested the establishment of technical chain for adapting to climate change, as well as the comprehensive layout, key directions and tasks of scientific and technological development for adapting to climate change.” (p. 3)
ad_past_outputs:
Cities: “In 216, China formulated an action plan for climate change adaptation in cities. In 217, the climate-resilient city pilot was launched in 28 cities. In each pilot area, a leading group for building climate-resilient cities was established, and a plan for urban adaptation to climate change was prepared. Adaptation actions that seek advantages and avoid disadvantages have been explored and implemented, including taking into account climate change in urban planning; improving urban monitoring, early warning and emergency response capabilities; carrying out adaptation actions in key areas such as infrastructure, water resources, natural ecosystems, and public health; exploring innovative systems and mechanisms for climate change adaptation, and strengthening international exchanges and cooperation in climate change adaptation.” (p. 22) 

Coastal erosion areas: “The China Sea Level Bulletin and the China Marine Disaster Bulletin are published every year. Seawall heightening and reinforcement projects have been implemented. Protection standards for coastal cities and major engineering facilities have been raised, while strategies for protecting coastal areas against sea level rise have been strengthened. Since 216, the Blue Bay Remediation Action has been carried out in coastal cities, improving marine ecological functions. In 217, warning tide levels in 11 coastal provinces were re-verified, and the technical methodology for risk assessment and zoning was developed for five risks, i.e. storm surges, tsunamis, sea ice, ocean waves, and sea level rise, which improve the level of scientific protection of coastal areas against marine disasters. In 22, China completed the First Scientific Assessment Report on the Ocean and Climate Change, which assessed the changes in China’s marine environment and the basic situation of sea level, and predicted the future trends of ocean and climate change.” (p. 23) 

Qinghai-Tibet Plateau: “Observation stations for plateau glaciers and frozen soils have been created, which also conducts the monitoring and forecasting of dam-burst floods in ice lakes. The system of nature reserves such as the Sanjiangyuan National Park has been strengthened to comprehensively protect the ecosystems of mountains, waters, forests, farmlands, lakes, grasslands, sands and ice. Grassland protection and development projects such as returning pasture to grassland have been implemented, effectively alleviating the degradation of alpine grassland. Integrated demonstration of ecological restoration technology system has been carried out, including ecological re-sowing and photovoltaic sprinkling of degraded grassland for adapting to climate change. As it is effective to mitigate the adverse effects of seasonal droughts, the practice was cited as a successful case of climate change adaptation, ecological restoration of alpine grasslands, and ecological function improvement in the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). To cope with the impacts of climate change on the Qinghai-Tibet Railway and other major projects, ground temperature monitoring was added along the Qinghai-Tibet Railway. Based on estimated future annual and seasonal warming characteristics of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and along the Qinghai-Tibet Railway, a variety of structural adaptation measures have been adopted to reduce the degradation of frozen soil and ensure the stability of frozen soil roadbed.” (p. 23) 

Other key ecological areas: “Highlighting vulnerability, sensitivity and main ecological functions, work has been planned for climate adaptation and ecological restoration in ecologically vulnerable areas, such as northwest agro-pastoral transition zone, southwest rocky desertification area, Yangtze River Basin, Yellow River Basin, and other major river and lake basins. Key areas with differences and their ecological vulnerabilities have been actively identified, taking into account the relative integrity of administrative regions and the relative consistency of climate change characteristics. Differentiated measures for ecological protection, management and restoration have been taken, such as comprehensive soil erosion management, vegetation restoration, land use adjustment, and natural forest protection plan, in order to optimize the adaptive allocation of water and soil resources, improve environmental carrying capacity, enhance ecosystem stability in ecologically vulnerable areas, and improve climate resilience in a coordinated manner.” (p. 23) 

Agriculture: “Great efforts have been made to promote research on agro-meteorological disaster prevention technologies and advance measures such as agricultural climate zoning and agricultural irrigation. More than 6 new technologies for agro-meteorological adaptation have been developed and promoted, such as disaster prevention and mitigation and production increase, and climate resource utilization. Through national key research and development plans, adaptation strategies for stable production have been explored, including sowing date adjustment, population optimization, and water and nitrogen migration. Crop varieties which are resistant to heat, drought, low light and low temperature are selected. Totally 3,564 agricultural climate zones at provincial, city and county levels and 5,33 agro-meteorological disaster risk zones have been delineated, which lays an important foundation for optimizing the agricultural structure and reducing losses from agricultural disasters. Effective irrigation area was enlarged from 55 million hectares in 25 to 68.3 million hectares in 219.” (p. 24) 

Forestry and grassland: “The Action Plan for Adaptation to Climate Change in the Forestry Sector (216–22) required more efforts in monitoring and early warning, risk management, and team building to comprehensively improve climate resilience of the forestry sector. A wildlife refuge system with national parks as the mainstay has been established. The protection and management of national public welfare forests, natural forests, and other types of forests has been strengthened, by strictly implementing forest land conservation and utilization plans at national, provincial and county levels and upgrading forest land quota management. The central government has arranged forestry funds to support the protection of natural forest resources, new-round return of farmland to forest and grassland, cultivation of forest resources, and compensations and subsidies for ecological benefits of forested wetland. In view of climate characteristics and grassland degradation in different regions, major grassland protection and restoration projects have been initiated, such as returning pasture to grassland, Beijing-Tianjin sandstorm source control, and artificial grass planting on degraded grassland, in an effort to speed up the restoration of degraded grassland vegetation and improve ecological functions and productivity of grassland. In severely overloaded and overgrazed areas, grazing ban through enclosure has been tightened, and combined with measures such as grass seed replanting, soil loosening and fertilizing, and rodent and pest control, to facilitate grassland recovery and vegetation restoration. Grassland that has been cultivated is returned to farmland in a planned way. The systems for grassland management and protection, grazing ban and suspension, and grass-livestock balance have been implemented to reduce the grazing pressure on natural grassland. In 219, the national grassland comprehensive vegetation coverage reached 56%; the total fresh-grass output of natural grasslands surpassed 1.1 billion tons; and the average livestock overload rate of key natural grasslands fell to 1.1%. The ecological functions of grassland, such as wind prevention and sand fixation, soil and water conservation, carbon fixation and oxygen release, and climate regulation, have been restored and strengthened, and the ecological environment in some grassland areas has been significantly improved.” (p. 24) 

Water resources: “The flood prevention and disaster reduction system has been perfected to enhance capability to guard against and cope with floods. Efforts have been made to speed up major river backbone projects, while accelerating the work to make up for weak links in flood control of small and medium-sized rivers. The responsibility system for flood control and drought relief has been improved, of which the core is that the administrative chief assumes full responsibility. A flood control and disaster mitigation system that combines structural measures such as reservoirs, dikes and flood storage and detention areas with non-structural measures has been basically formed. In a stronger move to build a water-saving society, the most stringent water resource management system has been put into effect, which contains three red lines for water use, water efficiency, and water pollution in water functional zones. Water resource storage and allocation projects have been implemented in river basins or regions. Regarding the construction of national water-saving cities, a total of 96 cities across the country have been recognized, whose annual water savings are about 5 billion m3 , equivalent to 1% of their annual water supply. Aquatic ecological protection and rural hydropower green development have made progress. River chief and lake chief systems have been fully implemented, and special action has been carried out to clear four behaviors (arbitrary occupation, mining, heap and construction), so that the national water environment and ecology and waterfront management and protection have been significantly improved. In 215, 3 pilot sponge cities were created, and to date, about 33, sponge city projects have been completed nationwide.” (p. 24-25) 

Public health: “The impacts of climate change on public health have been assessed, which takes into account the demand of traditional climate services and various industries including health for responding to climate change. The National Health Commission and departments concerned have compiled technical guidelines related to climate change and public health, such as guidelines for health protection in air pollution and environmental health emergencies in natural disasters, and 12 health and epidemic prevention guidelines and programs, including the investigation and control of infectious diseases in flood-stricken areas. They have also organized a series of research projects related to health risk assessment and adaptation to climate change, and formulated technical guidelines for health risk assessment of climate change.” (p. 25) 

Infrastructure: “Vigorous urban renewal projects have been launched, such as the transformation of old and dilapidated urban communities. Urban construction methods have been further changed by incorporating the transformation and upgrade of water supply, drainage and other pipe networks into urban renewal, and improving the green space of housing and surrounding areas. Prefabricated buildings have been promoted. In 219, nationwide 42 million m2 of prefabricated buildings were newly constructed, accounting for 13.4% of the newly added floor area. Urban greenways have effectively alleviated the urban heat island effect and related climate risks. As of 218, a total of 56, km of greenways have been built across the country. On the basis of analyzing the impacts and requirements of climate change on highway infrastructure construction, targeted measures are integrated in the design and construction process to improve project safety and durability. While strengthening the maintenance of transportation facilities, design and construction standards are continuously raised for roads, railways, airports, pipelines, urban rails, water buses, etc. With faster-pace transformation of old and dilapidated roads, improvement has been achieved in the resilience of national highway network to extreme weather such as low temperature, snow, floods, and typhoons.” (p. 25) 

Improving monitoring, early warning, and disaster prevention and mitigation capabilities: “The National Comprehensive Disaster Prevention and Mitigation Plan (216–22) was released to guide the work of disaster prevention, mitigation and relief in the context of climate change and strengthen the capacity building of climate disaster prevention and mitigation services. A comprehensive assessment model for climate change has been developed; a disaster information management system has been completed; and a nationwide long-time-series disaster database has been established, covering a variety of meteorological disasters such as regional droughts, heavy rain, heat, sand and dust, typhoons, snows, low temperature and freezing injury. Since 214, a total of over 19 billion yuan in the central government budget has been used to advance projects of meteorological satellites, radars, meteorological guarantees for mountain torrents and geological disasters, and marine meteorology. The layout of observation station network has been optimized, contributing to greater capability of monitoring and forecasting meteorological disasters and extreme weather and climate events. Emergency warning system functions have been improved and information dissemination channels broaden, thereby raising the public awareness of risk prevention. An air-ground-space integrated disaster monitoring system covering the whole country has been put in place, and the China Climate Change Monitoring Bulletin is issued every year. Urban areas have explored the establishment of inter-departmental early-warning information release centers, multi-hazard early warning systems, and risk management business systems. Rural areas have gradually accelerated the construction of meteorological disaster monitoring, early warning and emergency response systems.” (p. 26)
ad_past_invest: “In terms of adapting to climate change, the effective irrigation area of farmland in China expanded from 55 million hectares in 25 to 68.3 million hectares in 219, and the effective utilization coefficient of agricultural irrigation water increased from .45 to .56 in this period, which has enhanced climate resilience of agricultural production. Until June, 22, more than 3 billion m3 of water resources have been supplied to northern China via the eastern route and the middle route in Phase I of the South-North Water Diversion Project, improving its capability of northern China area to cope with the adverse effects of climate change. For key areas such as coastal provinces, vulnerability assessment, sea-level change impact investigation, and coastal erosion monitoring and evaluation have been conducted, and coastal shelterbelts and wave-proof projects have been carried out to enhance the resilience of coastal zones and coastal ecosystems to climate disasters.” (p. 4-5)
ad_coop:
China communicates information on international cooperation in Section IV: Promoting International Cooperation on Climate Change (p. 43-48). The section reports integrated information on mitigation and adaptation cooperation, but some adaptation-relevant highlights are presented below: 

Deepen South-South cooperation on climate change: “In the past five years, China has implemented the “1-1-1 Program” that provides financial, technology and capacity support to developing countries, such as least developed countries, small island developing states, and African countries, to help improve their capability to cope with climate change. This encompasses packaged projects, technical assistance, climate change mitigation and adaptation projects, donations of low-carbon, energy-efficient and environment-friendly materials and monitoring and early warning equipment, human resources development cooperation, and training courses on South-South cooperation on climate change. As of 219 year-end, under the framework of South-South cooperation, China has signed 38 memorandums of understanding with other developing countries to jointly build low-carbon demonstration zones, assisted 28 countries in 37 climate change mitigation and adaptation projects, and organized over 1 training courses on climate change, energy conservation and emission reduction that benefit more than 4, people.” (p. 45-46) 

Promote exchanges and cooperation with international organizations: “China has conducted extensive and practical cooperation on climate change with international financial institutions and international organizations, such as the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, New Development Bank, United Nations Development Programme, Global Environment Facility, and Green Climate Fund. As one of the 17 convening countries of the Global Commission on Adaptation, China has collaborated with the Global Center on Adaptation to open the China Office in June 219. Chinese Premier Li Keqiang, Dutch Prime Minister Mark Rutte, and former United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon attended the inauguration ceremony. In September 219, at the United Nations Climate Action Summit held in New York, China as the co-leader shared the positive progress in nature-based solutions, released the compendium of contributions, published the Nature-Based Solutions for Climate Manifesto, and proposed follow-up cooperation initiatives. China has also been deeply involved in the IPCC system construction and future planning, with 61 Chinese experts selected as authors of the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, ranking first among developing countries in number. In recent years, with focus put on issues of common concern for China and the world such as climate change, China has leveraged platforms such as the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development to promote the construction of a reasonable global environmental governance system. Actively participate in ship greenhouse gas emission reduction negotiations under the International Maritime Organization (IMO) framework, promote IMO to formulate a preliminary international ship greenhouse gas emission reduction strategy, and propose a constructive ship operation energy efficiency evaluation mechanism.” (p. 46-47)

“The updated NDC has been developed in accordance with the Decisions of the Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement 4/CMA.1, 1/CP.21, 9/CMA.1 and 18/CMA.1 by the Interagency Working Group under overall coordination of the Center of Hydrometeorological Service of the Republic of Uzbekistan and the support of the UN Development Program (UNDP) in Uzbekistan. Representatives of key ministries and agencies, academia and civil society, the private sector and youth took part in the development of the document.” (p. 5) 

“The NDC2 was developed based on the analytical framework used to develop the First Biennial Update Report (BUR1) of the Republic of Uzbekistan to the UNFCCC (2021), and reflects the results of mitigation measures that were widely discussed with all national stakeholders. The experience accumulated during the development and approval of the NDC1 served as the main background for the development and promotion of the NDC2. “In the future, the fulfillment of NDC commitments will be monitored in accordance with the documents under development: the National Adaptation Plan and Climate Change Strategy of the Republic of Uzbekistan, as well as the Biennial Transparency Report to the UNFCCC.” (p. 14) 

“An adaptation plan is currently under development. In accordance with state policy, with UNDP’s support and funding from the Green Climate Fund, the country has begun preparing the National Adaptation Plan (NAP). A road map has been developed to advance the NAP process.” (p. 22)
ad_coor_adp: “The Center of the Hydrometeorological Service of the Republic of Uzbekistan (Uzhydromet) is the National Focal Point for the UNFCCC and is responsible for fulfilling the country's commitments under the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement.” (p. 15)
ad_coor_other: “Uzbekistan has approved and is now implementing a five-year development strategy, the Action Strategy on Five Priority Areas for Development of the Republic of Uzbekistan in 217-221. The Strategy provides for the reduction of energy and resource intensity of the economy, widespread introduction of energy-saving technologies in production, increased use of renewable energy sources, which will help reduce GHG emissions; adoption of measures to mitigate the adverse impact of global climate change and the drying up of the Aral Sea on agricultural development and livelihoods of the population.” (p. 7)
ad_cc_short: “Since the early 195s, the average growth rate of air temperature throughout Uzbekistan has been .29°C every ten years, which is twice the rate of global warming.” (p. 6)
ad_impact_phys: “The situation is exacerbated by the continuing drying up of the Aral Sea, which has already lost 57% of its area, 8% of its volume and 64% of its depth in the last four decades. The Aral Sea basin now represents a salt desert called Aralkum, which adversely affects the ecology of the entire country. It is also expected that climate aridity will increase across the country, especially in its western part. The projected reduction in water resources and changing precipitation patterns will lead to even more prolonged droughts and extreme weather events.” (p. 21-22)
ad_impact_vul: “The most disadvantaged layers of the population live in the most arid regions of the country. Their livelihoods depend on agriculture and face increasing vulnerability to the impacts of climate change and the availability of natural resources. Under these conditions, the government has recognized the need to implement urgent adaptation measures and actions.” (p. 22)
ad_impact_cc:
“Climate change and impending water crisis, population growth, economic globalization and industrial development have a significant impact on the country's socio-economic systems. Climate-dependent sectors of the economy, such as agriculture, water and forestry, are most affected. Despite advances in irrigation and farming, weather remains a key influence factor on agricultural productivity, soil formation, and natural habitat.” (p. 21) 

“Water scarcity will increase significantly due to the projected decrease in water resources. The water scarcity in the country, which was 2 m3 in 25, is projected to increase to 7, m3 by 23 and to 13, m3 by 25. This will have an adverse impact on agriculture, particularly on the production of cotton, one of the country's main export products. The increased potential of evapotranspiration due to global warming causes a proportional increase in biological water demand in crops and, accordingly, increase in need for irrigation water. In the future, if demand for irrigation water will not be fully met due to water scarcity, crop yield reduction is expected. The expected loss of yield in a year of 9% water availability in the near future (239) under scenarios RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 can make up 1-13% for cotton, 1-13% for winter wheat, and 1- 12% for alfalfa.” (p. 22)

fairness_ambition:
"The equity, justice and ambition of this Contribution are analysed from various perspectives, with the understanding that there is no single indicator that can accurately reflect a globally equitable, fair and ambitious distribution of the parties' efforts. In the case of Argentina, the factors that explain the profile and trend of its emissions and removals do not respond to purely population or economic aspects, so that the indicators of emissions by intensity do not fully address the equity, justice and ambition of the country's efforts. Likewise, as a developing country vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, the Argentine Republic has the responsibility to promote actions and policies to achieve a model of sustainable, inclusive and balanced development, of a way that ensures that no one is left behind and is consistent with the 2030 Agenda and its Sustainable Development Goals."
"The Argentine Republic understands that an approach to the concepts of equity, justice and ambition must be made in the light of its national circumstances and on the basis of the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capacities."
objective: "The Second NDC of the Argentine Republic, as detailed in paragraphs 6.a and 6.b, is fair and ambitious, and reflects that the country's efforts are in line with the inputs and recommendations provided by science, with the collective efforts to achieve the objective of the Convention set forth in its article 2 and for the purpose of the Paris Agreement, in the light of national capacities and circumstances. It also reflects national priorities for long-term sustainable development, depending on the means of implementation necessary to implement it. Finally, in line with this objective and in accordance with the invitation of the Paris Agreement in its article 4.19 and in decision 1/CP.21, paragraph 35, the Argentine Republic will present in 2021 its Development Strategy with Low Greenhouse Gas Emissions in the Long Term."

ad_plan_ndc: National Climate Change Cabinet leads the coordinated and consensus-based design (4, 16). "Articulation and participation were central in the process of preparing this Second NDC. This document is the result of the joint work of 15 working groups of the national public administration, roundtables of federal articulation and working meetings with different sectors of society. All with the coordination of the National Cabinet of Climate Change (GNCC), this approach allowed to achieve the necessary consensus for the construction of a collective vision of the Argentine Republic by 23" (1). Bodies in NDC development: Meeting of Ministers presided over by the Minister Cabinet Chief; Focal Point Table made up of 15 working groups representing all areas of National Public Administration; Provincial Articulation Table representing each jurisdiction; Expanded Table with representatives from many public and private sector actors; Advisory Council composed of various experts and reps from many fields and sectors (17-18).
ad_plan_adp: A "clear and ambitious" National Adaptation and Mitigation Plan is under development led by National Climate Change Cabinet (4). The NAP is under development, guided by the Climate Change Law Article 16, which also establishes the obligation to develop the National Adaptation and Mitigation Plan, and Article 2, which establishes the formulation of jurisdictional-level Climate Change Response Plans. The NAP will be the key instrument for adaptation public policy in Argentina (66).
ad_coor_adp: National Climate Change Cabinet leads the coordinated and consensus-based design of policies for adaptation, including the NAP, defining the strategies, measures, policies and instruments to complete the objectives of the NAP and other policies (4, 16). The National Information System about Climate Change is a centralized tool for transparency and promotion of climate information for planning (16).
ad_cc_short: "In most of non-Patagonian Argentina, during the period 196-21  an increase in the average temperature of around .5 C was observed, with highs greater than 1C in various areas of Patagonia. Changes in the east and north of the country were also observed with respect to the frequency of extreme temperatures, fewer frosts and higher frequency of heat waves. In turn, the number of days a year with heat waves was doubled between 196 and 21, and a significant increase in the number of days with heat waves was observed, in particular in regions near the city of Buenos Aires" (42). "During the period of 196-21, increases in average annual rainfall were observed for most of Argentina's territory, with interannual and interdecadal variations. The largest nominal increases were recorded in specific areas of the east of the country, with more 2 mm/year, however, percentage increases were more significant in semi-arid areas" (42). "In the Patagonian Andes a negative variation in the average annual precipitation was observed for the period of 196–21. In the particular case of Cuyo, trends in the flow rates of some rivers in northern Mendoza and in San Juan throughout the twentieth century seem to indicate less precipitation in its high basins over the Cordillera" (43). "In the period of 196-21, there was an increase in the frequency and intensity of extreme precipitation events in the majority of the country, with higher values recorded in some areas, one of them being the wet littoral region.... in the west and most notably in the north, the dry winter periods have become longer. In these regions, rainfall in winter is scarce or null and therefore the increase in the maximum of consecutive dry days indicates a change towards an extension of the winter dry period" (43).
ad_cc_long: "by the end of the century an increase throughout the national territory is predicted, most notably in northwestern Argentina, with an increase of more than 3 C for a high-concentration scenario (RCP8.5) (PNAyM, 219)" (42).  "the strong interannual and interdecadal variability of rainfall is largely explained by the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomena, since in the region where Argentina is located, it causes above-average rainfall, and La Niña, which generates dry periods" (43). "For the higher concentrations scenario (RCP8.5), a decrease of between 1 and 2% in mean annual precipitation over western Patagonia and in the Mendoza mountain range, and an increase by the same amount in the center and most of the east of the country is projected for the end of the century. Also in line with what was recently observed, increases in the frequency of heavy rainfall events are projected" (43).
ad_impact_phys: "The Argentine Republic is a highly vulnerable country that needs to adapt given that it has a great diversity of areas susceptible to the effects of climate change: low-lying coastal [zones]; arid and semi-arid [zones]; [zones] with forest cover and exposed to forest deterioration; [zones] prone to disasters; [zones] exposed to drought and desertification; and [zones] with fragile ecosystems, including mountain ecosystems" (9,42). "Changes in rainfall had important implications for the region's water balance and hydrology. So, in the east and center province of Buenos Aires, southern Santa Fe and south of Corrientes, numerous fields have been transformed into permanent lagoons and water mirrors, such as the lagoons of Mar Chiquita in Cordoba and the Picasa in Santa Faith, which greatly increased its surface area" (43).  "[increase in dry winter periods] has created problems in the availability of water ...creating more favorable conditions for grassland and forest fires" (43). "If this trend [of decreased rainfall and river flows] continues, the availability of necessary water would be affected, for example, as a source of irrigation in the wine and fruit-growing activity" (43).  "[More frequent and intense extreme precipitation] resulted in more frequent flooding, [exacerbated] by inappropriate occupation and land use, resulting in areas with high exposure and vulnerability, and water works exposed to weather conditions different from those for which they were planned" (43). "[increase in dry winter periods] has created problems in the availability of water for some populations and for livestock activities" (43).  "From a border-frontier perspective, vulnerabilities are identified associated with shared resources, which also presents an opportunity for cooperation in the management of adaptation. In this sense, in the Plata Watershed, the hydroclimatic scenarios for principle water resources predict, by the end of the century, decreases in precipitations in High Paraguay, with impacts on water access,  agricultural producivity, generation of energy and on ecosystems; increases in precipitation--depending on the season of the year--in Low Paraguay, High Parana, Low Uruguay and the Plata River; and increases in precipitation throughout the year in High Uruguay, with associated impacts on increase in the frequency and intensity of riverbank floods and coastal erosion. Similar analyses were carried out in the Andes Mountain Range zone, where an increase in the risk of the loss of density and surface area of permanent snowfall areas is predicted, with very relevant effects in the hydrological patterns of the mountain range, and with affects on the access to water, on tourism, and on other productive activites, including fruit and wine horticulture" (47).

There will be increased impact on these communities due to their close relationship with nature and natural resources, the loss of biodiversity, the endemism of the ecosystems they inhabit, forced displacement from their territories, the fragility of their economic condition and their lack of participation in decision making" (44). "It is important to recognize that conditional factors based on gender, social dimension, ethnicity, age and religion, among others, influence the constuction and determination of vulnerabilities and capacities, generating differences and inequalities in facing and recovering from cliamte change impacts. Along the same line, the main index of work precarity and unemployment, income inequality as well as participation in low-productivity jobs, place women in a situation of increased vulnerability to disasters caused by climate change. Along the same line, the main index of work precarity and unemployment, income inequality as well as participation in low-productivity jobs, place women in a situation of increased vulnerability to disasters caused by climate change... informal settlements in urban zones are where women are found in the greatest state of vulnerability due to the lack of public services, deficiencies in houses, increased likelihood of suffering violent situations, which result in exacerbated situations of crisis. In the case of rural women, and their role simultaneously carrying out reproductive and productive work, they are facing the most barriers to development and commercialization of products and little experience in the management and use of credit. ad_impact_cc: Region-specific impacts: In NW Argentina (Salta, Jujuy, Tucumán, Santiago del Estero and Catamarca provinces) some populations will have difficulty accessing water, floods and water contamination are predicted to cause an increase in internal migration, increase in heat waves will have severe impacts in this region that is already socially vulnerable, human settlements in low-lying areas and urban areas could see health impacts like the propagation of disease vectors, more wildfires and stress on livestock, increase in agricultural diseases, acceleration of desertification, changes in range of species, adverse impacts on tourism due to temperature and algal or bacteria outbreaks, increased pressure on existing infrastructure like electricity generation during heat waves, increase in damage to infrastructure due to floods, and glacier retreat (43-44). In NE Argentina ( Chaco, Corrientes, Formosa, Entre Ríos, Misiones and Santa Fe provinces) there will be an increased risk of vector-borne illnesses (dengue, yellow fever, leishmaniasis), floods will impact population health and infrastructure and rural livelihoods, internal migration, low water levels in rivers will make potable water harder to find and impact fishing and subsistence, indigenous communities will be especially impacted, loss of cultivars (soy, sunflower, cotton, corn, wheat, rice) and increase of agricultural diseases, risks to production systems, risks to animal and human health due to high temperatures, increase in periods of extreme drought that result in animal die-offs that especially impact small-scale livestock producers, erosion of soils due to droughts and extreme rainfall as well as deforestation and degradation, increase in the impacts of heat waves especially on the most vulnerable (44). In the Cuyo Region (Mendoza, San Juan, La Rioja and San Luis provinces) there will be increased and prolonged periods of water scarcity impacting all sectors and especially already-vulnerable communities and agriculture, restrictions in irrigation for olive and wine and fruit farming as well as for hydroelectricity, increase in extreme drought periods that lead to wildfires and loss of flora and fauna, increase in extreme flooding (45). In the regions of Patagonia and North Patagonia ( La Pampa, Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut, Santa Cruz, Tierra del Fuego, Antártida and Islas del Atlántico Sur Provinces) there will be diminished river flow and water availability that impacts tourism and irrigation and hydroelectricity, risks of floods and loss of infrastructure due to sea level rise, increase frequency and intensity of extreme events, increased exposure of homes and infrastructure to extreme events, impacts on the electrical system and communications systems, increase in droughts and desertification, increased risk of soil erosion and desertification impacting agriculture, negative impacts on mountaineering and skiing tourism, increased risk of avalanches, loss of scenic resources due to glacier retreat, increase in periods of extreme drought leading to wildfires and flora and fauna loss, increased vectors and vector-borne diseases (45). In the Central Region (Buenos Aires and Córdoba) there will be increased frequency and duration of heat waves, increased social vulnerability to extreme heat events especially in heat islands, pressures on infrastructure, losses in livestock agriculture due to floods and droughts, sea level rise in all sea coast provinces, increased impacts of floods on rural communities, coastal erosion and SLR impacts across sectors, public service infrastructure impacted by increase in the Silver River, increased damages on homes and infrastructure in low-lying zones due to floodings especially in informal settlements, increased presence of vectors and vector-borne diseases (dengue, zika, chikunguna), acceleration of desertification, increase in periods of extreme drought with cross-cutting impacts (45).
ad_vision: "In order to adapt ourselves to new climate scenarios, strengthening awareness, capacity-building and implementation of  vulnerability-reduction measures for communities, infrastructure and productive systesm are aimed for" (5). "Around 23, all Argentinians will have knowledge about the adverse effects of climate change, the corresponding adaptation measures, and will have built capacities that allow them to respond in solidarity to this urgent challenge to protect the planet. The climate policy of Argentina will have achieved an increase in adaptation capacity, strengthened resilience and decreased vulnerability of distint local governments and social, economic and environmental sectors, through measures that, among others, prioritize communities and social groups in vulnerable situations and will incorporate a gender focus and intergenerational equity. This process will be based in the best scientific knowledge available and will be able to generate co-benefits with mitigation, as applicable. All of this will be with a vision to contribute to sustainable development, build a more equitable, just, and in-solitarity society, and achieve a climate change response that is adequate and compatible with the objectives of the Paris Agreement" (48).

"In terms of raising awareness, a discussion was held to integrate the gender perspective into the agenda of the climate change, which included views from government management and from science. The discussion was directed to the general public and had the participation of youth organizations that work to raise awareness and public consciousness in the fight against climate change. A training course on "Gender and Climate Change" was also held to integrate this perspective in the NAP. The course was aimed at all the personnel of the National Directorate of Climate Change and was aimed at introduce the subject from its more general notions to more specific conceptual and methodological issues related to how to mainstream gender issues in adaptation. These courses are considered to be especially important, since gender relations can be sources of social inequalities, both internally organizations, as well as the actions that are promoted from them. Based on the results and conclusions of these awareness-raising and training instances, an initial identification of socioeconomic vulnerabilities with a gender perspective was carried out, as well as the categorization of the adaptation measures according to their differential impact on genders. This was a fundamental advance to reflect how the gender perspective can become an integral axis of a climate policy. Also within the framework of capacity building, a course on monitoring and evaluation (M&E) system took place with the aim of applying it to the PNA. In this sense, the medium-term objective is to achieve the implementation of an M&E system that takes into account gender considerations in the monitoring and evaluation of adaptation policies. Likewise, ties were strengthened with the Ministry of Women, Gender and Diversity, in order to define lines of joint work; and contacts were initiated with technical teams from other countries that allowed the sharing strategies, methods and instruments for incorporating the gender perspective, as well as making visible the obstacles and challenges emerging during the process. These relations actions also made it possible to establish potential work commitments at the regional level to advance gender and climate policies" (72). "A robust legal and programmatic framework and consensus among all political parties has been established, embodied in the National Climate Change Law, which strategically integrates adaptation. Based on the National Climate Change Law, a new institutional framework of a transversal nature has been established for climate action, including adaptation, with the implementation of a National Climate Change Cabinet. The main adaptation measures of the country have been established by legal means. A national planning process has been established by legal means that develops the National Adaptation and Mitigation Plan, and that includes the National Adaptation Plan, which is currently being formulated. A subnational planning process has been established by legal means, in which each jurisdiction is responsible for develop Response Plans that strategically integrate adaptation" (72).

ad_me_ins: "The vehicle for monitoring the adaptation process of Argentina will be the National Adaptation and Mitigation Plan (PNAyMCC) through its own monitoring and evaluation (M&E) system. The purpose of the system is to monitor the progress of the implementation and the results of the PNAyMCC and identify improvements in the management of the adaptation process for learning and improvement keep going. The M&E system in the PNAyMCC will be applied at the national level. However, general indicators will be formulated in conjunction with the Federal Council on the Environment (COFEMA) for the subnational level. This system will, in turn, enable monitoring of the effectiveness of the adaptation process, provide appropriate information to decision-making--thus improving governance--specify information on new or greater needs for resources for adaptation, and identify areas for improvement, among others. Likewise, said system will allow the disaggregation of information by gender. Finally, the system will allow the generation of relevant information in relation to the impacts of climate change and adaptation in accordance with the provisions of the Enhanced Framework on Transparency of Action and Support (article 13 of the Paris Agreement), whose guidelines on adaptation were included in Chapter IV of the Annex to Decision 18 / CMA1 in general, and in its sections E and F in particular" (82-83).

New Zealand will continue to account for all deforestation emissions. b. Forests established before the activity start year will continue to be accounted for under a business-as-usual reference level, as per the Kyoto Protocol, to address the dynamic effects of age structure resulting from activities and practices before the reference year, and the ongoing cycles of forest harvest and regrowth that occur as part of normal, sustainable forest management in production forests. c. fairness_ambition: "New Zealand is responsible for low levels of emissions now and historically (0.17 per cent of global gross emissions in 2017). Countries which each individually contribute one per cent or less of global emissions account for nearly a quarter of total emissions. Therefore, New Zealand’s efforts matter. The likely cost to the New Zealand economy of meeting this NDC target in terms of GDP is high relative to many other Parties. This is due to a number of factors, such as the existing high level of renewable electricity generation (80-85 per cent), and the make-up of our emissions profile, where almost half of our total emissions originate from agriculture. New Zealand’s domestic 2050 target under the CCRA places an emphasis on long-lived gases. The target is to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to net zero by 2050 (excluding biogenic methane for which the target is 24-47 per cent below 2017 levels). The outcome we seek for the ‘form’ or ‘type’ of contribution we deliver is an NDC that provides a fair, comparable and transparent representation of New Zealand’s effort on climate change. Different forms of contribution will better facilitate the accurate measurement of reductions to track progress towards a country’s global goal than others, or more clearly (or fairly) represent a country’s “effort” (depending on their national circumstance). We consider that New Zealand’s updated NDC, and particularly the fact that it will be achieved via a budget for the period is the right form for facilitating accurate measurement of New Zealand’s effort."
objective: "New Zealand welcomed the IPCC’s Special Report on global warming of 1.5°C, and the AR6 Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis, which emphasised the urgency of climate action that we have a duty to respond to. New Zealand’s target choice is primarily guided by the best available scientific knowledge. The IPCC is the definitive source of evidence to support climate change policy development. The IPCC reports represent the best expert assessment of global knowledge on climate change. The AR6 Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis is the most up to date report from the IPCC on the physical science of climate change. The report makes clear that it is “unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land”, and caused “widespread and rapid changes in the atmosphere, ocean, cryosphere and biosphere”. The scale of these changes is unprecedented over centuries to thousands of years. New Zealand has a duty to respond to the report’s findings that “global warming of How the nationally determined contribution contributes towards Article 2, paragraph 1(a), and Article 4, paragraph 1, of the Paris Agreement. (i.e. global temperature goals, including to limit global temperature to 1.5°C): 17 1.5°C and 2°C will be exceeded during the 21st century unless deep reductions in CO2 and other greenhouse gas emissions occur in the coming decades”. The Special Report on global warming of 1.5°C emphasises that limiting global warming to 1.5°C will “require rapid and far-reaching transitions” in most human activities. The report provides emissions pathways consistent with limiting warming to 1.5°C, which have gained considerable influence as representing what is “necessary” to achieve the aim of the Paris Agreement. The Special Report on global warming of 1.5°C provided evidence to inform the 2050 target in New Zealand’s Climate Change Response Act, which will be a significant challenge requiring early and more ambitious action across all sectors. The Act has legislated a domestic target that contributes to the global effort under the Paris Agreement to limit global warming to 1.5°C. In May 2021 the Climate Change Commission provided advice that New Zealand’s NDC was not compatible with contributing to global efforts to limit global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. The Commission advised in order to be more likely to be compatible, the contribution New Zealand makes over the NDC period should reflect a reduction of net emissions of much more that 36 per cent below 2005 gross levels by 2030, with the likelihood of compatibility increasing as the NDC is strengthened further. New Zealand’s updated NDC of a reduction of 50 per cent below gross 2005 levels by 2030 is aligned with this advice to have greater compatibility with contributing to global efforts to limit global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels."

ad_plan_ndc: “This document constitutes the revised NDC of the Union of the Comoros for 2030. It is the result of an inclusive and transparent process, which lasted just over a year, helping to enhance the country's ambition in the fight against climate change by taking into account: 1) New orientations of national development policies and strategies such as the Emerging Comoros Plan and the strategy of accelerated growth and sustainable development; 2) New priorities and costs in terms of priority climate-related investments; 3) Analyzes of new sectors and gases to be considered and integrated into greenhouse gas inventories” (p. 1)
ad_plan_adp: “The participatory review exercise of the NDC made it possible to update and expand the adaptation objectives, monitoring indicators and targets up to 23 for the sectors identified as the most vulnerable to CC in the Comoros (agriculture, biodiversity, forest, fisheries and coastal and marine ecosystems, water resources, health and economic and social infrastructure). In addition, the cross-cutting sectors of disaster risk reduction and the integration of adaptation and awareness-raising were also prioritized.” (p. 8)
ad_coor_other: “In its revised general policy document for the period 218-221, the Strategy for Accelerated Growth and Sustainable Development (SCA2D), the Comorian government intends to reconcile structural transformation and diversification of the economy with the sustainable management of natural resources and resilience, especially of the agricultural sector and rural communities, to natural disasters and the effects of climate change. Adaptation is also found in the ambition of the newly adopted Comoros Emerging Plan 23 (PCE), which aims to make Comoros by 23: ‘a country resilient to shocks in all dimensions of sustainable development’.” (p. 8)
ad_cc_short: “The Country is particularly vulnerable to climate change, like all the other small island developing states (PIED): analyses of meteorological data have shown the existence of climate change manifested by a gradual decrease in rainfall, a trend increasing annual temperature, rising sea level, increased aridity and more drought.” (p. 2)
ad_cc_long: “Projections obtained from the use of global climate models show an increasing trend in temperatures as well as an increase in the number of hot days. The mean annual temperature is therefore expected to increase from .8 (RCP 2.6) to 2.1 ° C (RCP 8.5) by 26 and from 1.2 (RCP 2.6) to 3.6 ° C (RCP 8.5) by by 29. The seasonal projections predict a decrease in seasonal precipitation, and an increase in precipitation during the rainy season.” (p. 7)
ad_impact_phys: “At the same time, the frequencies of extreme climatic and meteorological events such as tropical storms, floods, heat waves and drought episodes have slightly increased and constitute the main hazards impacting the Union of the Comoros. Combined with anthropogenic pressures (deforestation, land degradation, sand extraction, obsolete agricultural practices, etc.) exerted on natural resources, these hazards are likely to strongly compromise the development efforts undertaken by the country in recent years and accentuate the vulnerability of certain ecosystems and groups of already fragile populations.” (p. 2)
ad_impact_vul: “The other sources of the country's vulnerability are linked to: 1) an incidence of poverty which varies from one island to another and which seems to be higher in rural areas; 2) an estimated unemployment of 3.7% in 218 but which particularly affects young people (8.5%) and women (4.6%); 3) relatively high demographic growth (2.24% in 218) 2 but which is however lower than that of GDP (3.43% in 218).” (p. 3)
ad_impact_cc:
“Agriculture and biodiversity are the sectors most vulnerable to climate change, followed by forests, coastal areas, fisheries, water resources, health, and economic and social infrastructure.” (p. 2) 

“The results of the vulnerability analyses carried out so far in the Comoros show that the sectors most vulnerable to climate change are agriculture and biodiversity (very high vulnerability), forestry, coastal areas, fishing, water resources, health and economic and social infrastructure (high vulnerability). A vulnerability analysis of each of these sectors is presented in the technical report annexed to this revised NDC. This vulnerability is likely to increase for most of these sectors, which need urgent action to cope with the effects of climate change.” (p. 8)

“The Union of the Comoros will need an overall envelope of more than EUR 1,31 million to carry out the implementation of its NDC, i.e. around an average annual amount of EUR 13 million, of which at least 92 million EUR for mitigation measures and EUR 399 million for adaptation measures. Given its very limited resources, the Union of the Comoros cannot undertake its measures without the help of the international community, in particular within the framework of the technological and financial support effort between countries promoted by the Paris Agreement but also through the Green Climate Fund, funding from multilateral or bilateral partners, or other existing or future funding mechanisms, including from the private sector or from transfers from the diaspora.” (p. 13)
ad_nonfin: “The Union of the Comoros is counting on the international community to consolidate the efforts undertaken for more than 2 years in the fight against climate change. Indeed, international support in the form of funding, capacity building and technology transfer is necessary to support the implementation of the revised NDC” (p. 13)
ad_me_ins: “As for adaptation measures, their monitoring will be done through existing sectoral working groups. The establishment of a single, institutionalized and centralized monitoring system for the various technical and political aspects of the NDC is envisaged and should be quickly supported. The results of this monitoring will be communicated to the stakeholders involved in the implementation of the NDC and to decision-makers (at the local, sectoral, national level) allowing them, if necessary, to take corrective adjustment measures.” (p. 12)
ad_ref: Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) (p. 1)
ad_gen_diff:
“The integration of the gender dimension, in the implementation of this new NDC, reflects the concern of the Comorian government to better take into account the important role that the Comorians play in many sectors strongly impacted by climate change such as the agriculture, water and forest management, health, disaster risk reduction as well as the specific impacts they suffer from their roles and responsibilities which differ from those of men in Comorian society.” (p. 1) 

“In rural areas, women's livelihoods depend largely on natural resources (water, forest products, agriculture) which are highly dependent on climatic hazards. The impacts of CC (land and forest degradation, erosion, water stress, natural disasters) lead to the scarcity of resources making more difficult the activities carried out by women. Women's difficult access to economic and productive resources further weakens their ability to adapt to climate change.” (p. 11)
ad_gen_par:
“In 28, the country adopted a National Policy on Gender Equity and Equality (PNEEG) which aims to give priority to a better participation of women in economic development activities, in decision-making activities that they be political, traditional or religious, to the capacity building of women and girls, the right to education, the right to health, the legal status and the application of the fundamental rights of women and girls.” (p. 1) 

“The vision of the government of the Union of the Comoros is to "make the Comoros an emerging country by 23, respectful of human rights, gender equality and promoting the rule of law". Thus, in 217, the law on the parity law establishing a quota of at least 3% of women in elective and nominative positions was adopted to, among other things, encourage the political participation of women and their representation in electoral processes.” (p. 1)
ad_gen_invest: “The initiatives carried out in recent years by the Comorian government with the support of development partners are helping to strengthen the empowerment of women by offering them more economic opportunities and income-generating activities. Likewise, efforts are being made in terms of gender parity in capacity building activities. Specifically, the Comorian government has set up projects in the field of agriculture with an environmental impact, including the fight against climate change, in which 45% of the beneficiaries are women. The latter, like men, have been sensitized on issues related to climate change, received training and had access to more efficient tools and techniques in agriculture. The National Emergency Preparedness and Response Plan took gender into account in the education and protection sector, which should result in the 'establishment of mechanisms for monitoring and sensitizing displaced populations of the various forms of abuse, violence and sexual exploitation, prevention of abuse, violence and sexual exploitation of children and women, taking into proper charge of each of the identified vulnerable groups by providing the essential human and material resources and the establishment of basic protection and supervision structures adapted and accessible to vulnerable groups, especially women and children'.” (p. 11)
ad_gen_me: “Gender-specific analyzes will be carried out in order to better understand the qualitative differences between women and men, girls and boys and to better take into account the needs, rights and priorities of each. Monitoring will incorporate the systematic collection of data disaggregated by sex and age to monitor the gender-sensitive impact of climate change actions and the effectiveness of gender mainstreaming initiatives. Gender-specific baselines and indicators will be defined to monitor progress on gender equity.” (p. 12)
ad_econloss_cur: “The vulnerability study carried out in 218 estimated the losses caused by damage from natural disasters deemed to be major at .39% of average GDP over the period 198 - 217. However, this figure is an average over the period considered and does not reflect the heterogeneity and all the damage caused by the different events due to lack of data” (p. 2)
ad_econloss_fu: “Without ambitious measures, the cost of climate-related impacts was estimated in 214 at US $836 million by 25, i.e. an average annual cost over the period of US $23 million which, reduced to 219 GDP would represent 1.9%.” (p. 2)
ad_ldin_eve: “Sea level has risen between +1 and +6 mm / year since 1992 in the Indian Ocean region. This sea level is also expected to increase by 4 mm per year over the next fifty years, corresponding to a potential average rise of 2 cm by 25, twice the rise observed over the last hundred years. (2 to 25 cm). This rise in sea level, combined with coastal erosion, threatens coastal ecosystems, coastal forests, equipment and infrastructure, especially roads, and most coastal communities.” (p. 8)

ad_plan_ndc:
“The update of the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela was carried out through a broad, systematic and multisectoral participatory process for the joint construction and validation of sectoral commitments, led by the MINEC through the General Directorate for Adaptation and Mitigation of Climate Change, as Technical Focal Point before the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).” (p. 153) 

“In order to ensure the participation of all key sectors of Venezuela in updating the second NDC, MINEC designed an action plan with execution activities in the years 2020-2021; taking the following actions, namely: 1) A Workshop on Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) was held in the context of unilateral coercive measures and SARS-CoV-2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus). 2, Coronavirus type 2 of severe acute respiratory syndrome) or COVID 19, represent for Venezuela to respond in this context to the commitments assumed for the reduction of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and adaptation to climate change, accordingly to the provisions of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the 2015 Paris Agreement. 2) Inter-institutional coordination and articulation with the different sectors. 3) Inter-institutional liaison was established for the compilation of information and interaction with each sector. 4) 26 working meetings were held with external sectors and 11 working meetings with the internal substantive Directorates of Minec, which made it possible to thoroughly review the needs and barriers to overcome for the implementation of the NDC. It is important to note that, in compliance with the mobility and biosafety restriction measures due to the health crisis caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, the sessions were mostly held in virtual mode. 5) Elevation of the NDC in the different sectors and advance in their implementation.” (p. 153) 

“The collaborative work consisted of: (1) bibliographic review and analysis of political and national development priorities; (2) preliminary preparation of possible commitments on climate change and their prioritization; (3) successive work meetings of the technical teams until a consensus is reached regarding the scope, structure, follow-up mechanisms, among other operational aspects of each commitment; (4) various consultations via telephone, email, via zoom for each sector to expand actions to face the climate crisis; (5) space for socialization and feedback through meetings; (6) technical-political approval process of all parties involved.” (p. 153-154)
ad_coor_adp:
“In this sense, on January 16, 219, the Ministry of Popular Power for Ecosocialism (MINEC), as the National Environmental Authority, created in its organizational structure the "General Directorate for Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation" whose objective is to promote the participation, awareness, systematization and consolidation of actions for the conservation and protection against the effects of Climate Change, through the design and implementation of policies and guidelines applied at the national level, in terms of adaptation, mitigation and associated losses and damages. This General Directorate is the Technical Focal Point before the UNFCCC, and also seeks to strengthen Ecosocialism as an axiological value of environmental management in the field of the fight against Climate Change, deepening the sustainable political, economic and social model, assumed in a way collective and responsible with nature. To implement these tasks, the General Directorate was structured into four Line Directions: Climate Change Adaptation Directorate; Climate Change Mitigation Directorate; Directorate of Policy Formulation, Monitoring and Control of Climate Change; and the Directorate of Losses and Damages due to Climate Change.” (p. 25) 

“Coordination efforts at the national level are carried out through the National Coordinating Committee for Civil Protection and Disaster Administration, which is made up of all the offices of the National Executive and which groups together the sectors and levels of government, with the participation of the representation of state governors, mayors and non-governmental organizations, as well as the National Coordination of Firefighters and civilian emergency management agencies. The Committee also provides for the constitution of sectoral technical subcommittees and specialized work teams for actions and measures in the field of civil protection and disaster management.” (p. 89) 

“The [NDC update] process was coordinated by the Management team of the General Directorate for Adaptation and Mitigation of Climate Change as speakers / facilitators, and had the methodological support and guidance derived from the international forums and workshops in which our country participated in the virtual mode.” (p. 153)

ad_impact_phys:
“The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela is a country vulnerable to different natural phenomena, earthquakes, floods, mass movements, tropical storms and hurricanes, tsunamis and technological events, such as fires, explosions, spills and others. The record of historical events reflects that the highest incidence and impacts, 71% of them, occur as a result of events triggered by rains.” (p. 128-129) 

Ecosystems (Coastal Zone, Territorial Planning, Mountains, Wetlands): “In the country, climate variability and the occurrence of extreme events have been more prone in recent years, in the same way it is difficult to forecast precise effects of climate change; However, recent studies warn about the potential impacts on humans due to floods, storms, droughts and heat waves, with predictions of lack of drinking water and possible conflicts due to increasing competition for water resources, as well as large changes in conditions for food production. Climate change has a clear impact on water supply, affecting ecosystems (in low-lying areas, island areas, low-lying coastal areas, arid and semi-arid areas, areas exposed to floods, drought and desertification, and areas with ecosystems fragile mountainous) and agriculture.” (p. 139) 

Biodiversity (Conservation and Use of Sustainable Biodiversity): “Climate change has a clear impact on biodiversity. This constitutes a threat to individuals, species and ecosystems; on the other hand, impacts on biodiversity can alter the structure and functioning of ecosystems, and their interactions with biological, geochemical and hydrological cycles (IPCC, 27). A determining factor is any natural or anthropic factor that causes, directly or indirectly, a change in an ecosystem or in biodiversity. Those that have an explicit influence are direct determining factors. These include changes in land use, climate change, the presence of invasive species, overexploitation of natural resources, and pollution.” (p. 147)
ad_impact_cc:
Urban Settlements (Housing): “Climate change is affecting the natural variability of the climate, causing extreme events to take place more and more frequent and intense, and consequently, the loss of human life and damage to property are increasing.” (p. 15) 

Health: “Climate Change represents a risk to human health, due to the increase in environmental health factors (physical, chemical and biological), for example: heavy rainfall and floods, increased temperatures and relative humidity, favor the appearance of vectors and reservoirs of parasites or viruses that cause metaxenic diseases, contamination of supply water sources, affecting their quality, greenhouse gas emissions, among others” (p. 13) 

Labor (Social Justice): “All work entities, regardless of their economic activity, are exposed to the effects of climate change, where serious consequences are evident in terms of direct and indirect job losses, in this sense, workers' organizations to address these effects; (Workers 'Productive Committee (CPT), Prevention Delegates, Trade Unions, Workers' Councils, among others), must develop actions to mitigate and adapt to it.” (p. 134)
ad_vision: “In this sense, the objectives must be achieved as appropriate: 1) Reduce vulnerability to the effects of climate change by building adaptive capacity and resilience. 2) Facilitate the integration of climate change adaptation, in a coherent manner, into relevant new and existing policies, programs and activities, in particular development planning processes and strategies, in all relevant sectors and at different level.” (p. 89)

“Since 2019, like the other countries that are parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, Niger has been revising and strengthening its NDC through the ''Climate Actions Enhancement Package'' (CAEP) initiative of the NDC Partnership. This revision is under the leadership of the ministry in charge of the environment. The latter is assisted in this task by the focal points of the AFOLU and Energy sectors, research and training institutions and civil society organizations federated by the national committee for the revision and strengthening of the NDC.” (p. 1) 

“The revision of the NDC aims to capitalize on the achievements of the implementation of the first NDC and to fill in the gaps thanks to the multifaceted support of the member partners of NDC Partnership who are currently financing studies relating to governance and the implementation operational work of the NDC. The deliverables resulting from these studies were validated by two (2) bodies, namely the technical sub-committee and the National Committee in charge of reviewing and strengthening the NDC. The validated documents served as the basis for the formulation of the revised NDC which will be submitted to the UNFCCC by the Government of Niger as a prelude to the COP26 on Climate in November 2021 in Glasgow, Scotland.” (p. 1-2)
ad_cc_short:
“Since the 195s, Niger's climate has experienced 3 distinct rainfall cycles, common to the entire Sahel: 1) between the 195s and 197s, Niger enjoyed a cycle of wet years; 2) between the 197s and 199s, Niger was confronted with a cycle of major droughts, marked by particularly dry episodes in 197 and 1984, as in the rest of the Sahel; 3) from the beginning of the 199s, much better rainfall conditions returned to this region (Ali et al., 28, 21), accompanied however by an increase in the interannual variability of rainfall.” (p. 9) 

Precipitation: “Figure 1 below represents the simulated evolution of the average accumulations of precipitation during the rainy season (JJAS) over the short term (top) and the medium term (bottom), for the RCP4.5 scenarios (at left) and RCP 8.5 (right). The models predict a general upward trend in cumulative precipitation during the rainy season (JJAS) compared to the 1981-21 climatological reference. These conclusions are consistent with the trends obtained by different authors. According to the models, the increase in rainfall should be greater in the North and East of the country. The increase in rainfall should be greater in the medium term compared to the short term, and all the more so in a pessimistic scenario of an increase in greenhouse gases (RCP 8.5 compared to RCP 4.5 ).” (p. 9-1) 

Temperature: “The models tend to show a trend towards a decrease in the number of rainy days during the JJAS period throughout Niger. The decrease in the number of rainy days is greater in the medium term compared to the short term, but similar between the RCP 4.5 and 8.5 scenarios. In Niger, the combination of an increase in total rainfall (Figure 2) and a decrease in the number of rainy days over the JJAS season (Figures 1) indicates a trend towards intensification of rainfall and increased rainfall. the duration of dry spells during the agricultural season [...] The models tend to show a trend towards a decrease in the number of rainy days during the JJAS period throughout Niger. The decrease in the number of rainy days is greater in the medium term compared to the short term, but similar between the RCP 4.5 and 8.5 scenarios. In Niger, the combination of an increase in total rainfall (Figure 2) and a decrease in the number of rainy days over the JJAS season (Figures 1) indicates a trend towards intensification of rainfall and increased rainfall. the duration of dry spells during the agricultural season.” (p. 1-11)
ad_impact_phys:
“In view of this situation, Niger is faced with extreme climatic hazards which are becoming more frequent and violent (recurrent and successive droughts, floods, violent winds, extreme temperatures and sand or dust storms; the variability of rains increase and its poor distribution in time and space; the persistence of other indirect factors such as epidemics (meningitis, cholera), crop enemies (miner caterpillars, flower insects, aphids, seed-eating birds), diseases for livestock (epizootics), bush fires, etc.” (p. 9) 

“In terms of impact on agriculture, attacks by the Desert Locust and other crop pests have damaged more than 1.6 million hectares. The hazards (drought, bush fires, floods) together account for more than 1 million hectares. More than 17 million head of cattle also perished during the events between 21 and 214.” (p. 11) 

Forestry: “Reduction of biodiversity; Degradation of forest ecosystems; Disappearance of certain animal and plant species; Proliferation of harmful terrestrial and aquatic species (water hyacinth, Sida cordifolia, Tipha autralis); Formation of ravines and/or sand dunes, the soil pollution, crusting; Migration of wildlife; Decreased productivity of forest potential.” (p. 19) 

Water Resources: “Floods (diluvian rains); Violent wind, sandstorm; Extreme temperature; Droughts; Pollution of surface and underground waters; Variations in piezometric levels; Increasingly rapid drying up of rivers” (p. 2)
ad_impact_cc:
“Like other West African countries, Niger is very vulnerable to climate change, characterized by high climatic variability and rainfall that leads to recurrent rainfall deficits. These deficits result in very harmful repetitive and cyclical droughts. The phenomena of desertification and the degradation of natural resources and land have been a major concern for the economic and social development of the country for decades.” (p. 7) 

“All these extreme climatic events constitute an obstacle to achieving the objectives of the fight against poverty and for economic and social development as set out in policies and strategies (SDDCI-235, PDES, 3N Initiative, PNEDD-216, SPN2A , etc). This situation constitutes a major challenge to be met.” (p. 12) 

Agriculture: “Reduction of rainwater resources; Resurgence of crop enemies (desert locusts, grasshoppers, leaf miners, etc.); Reduction/loss of crop yield and production; Disruption of the crop calendar (preparation, sowing, maintenance work, harvest , etc.); Silting of agricultural land, reduction in the contribution of agriculture to GDP; Silting of oasis basins; Local flooding of riparian areas of water bodies causing loss of crops, loss of agricultural production and stocks, damage to agricultural infrastructure and irrigation schemes; Increase in potential evapotranspiration; Conflicts between rural producers; Degradation of ecosystems; Accentuation of food and nutritional insecurity” (p. 17-18) 

Livestock: “Change in the composition of herds through a gradual replacement of cattle by small ruminants and camels, which are more resistant to difficult climatic conditions; Reconversion of nomadic herders into sedentary populations; Generalized reduction in fodder potential; Silting of pastoral areas; Proliferation of certain plant species not palatable to animals (Sida cordifolia, Calotropis procera); Degradation of rangeland; Increase in the mortality of livestock, especially cattle, linked to recurrent droughts; Fall in income for breeders; Reduction in the contribution of livestock to GDP.” (p. 19)

Monitoring and evaluation will be carried out by a Permanent Secretariat housed at the ME/LCD and will be done in a participatory manner with all the representatives of the policy body responsible for implementing the NDC. planning_processes: "The emission reduction target of at least minus 50 per cent by 2030 has been approved by the Swiss Parliament in 2016. Comprehensive consultation proceedings for both the second CO2 Act and the ratification of the Paris Agreement including the 2030 target had preceded the parliamentary debate, allowing stakeholders in Switzerland to comment on the target and the implementation plan. The ratification of the Paris Agreement passed the parliamentary process in 2017, after the deadline for a facultative referendum expired. After parliamentary debate, both chambers adopted the third CO2 Act on 25 September 2020. However, the third CO2 Act was subject to a facultative referendum in June 2021 and was rejected by the Swiss population, following months of public debate. Immediately following the referendum, in December 2021, Parliament has adopted a prolongation of the second CO2 Act with an annual emission reduction target of 1.5 per cent per year compared to 1990 levels for the period 2021 to 2024. In March 2024, Parliament approved a new version of the third CO2 Act, entering into force on 1 January 2025. This revision sets the targets for 2030 for national total as well as sectoral emissions and provides for policies and measures to reach these targets. The ordinance implementing the third CO2 Act underwent public consultation from July to October 2024."

Given the low greenhouse gas intensity of Switzerland today, this NDC represents a high level of ambition for 2030."
